Where it began

Kapil Dev's story starts in Chandigarh, where he was born on 6 January 1959, and he went to D. A. V. College there. He made his first-class debut for Haryana in November 1975 and announced himself straight away, taking six wickets as Punjab were bowled out for 63. By the end of that first season he had 121 wickets in 30 matches.

His Test debut came at Faisalabad on 16 October 1978. Within months he had his first Test hundred, 126 against the West Indies in Delhi, made in just 124 balls.

The player

He played 131 Tests and took 434 wickets at 29.65, with 23 five-wicket innings and a best of 9 for 83 against the West Indies at Ahmedabad. He also made 5,248 runs at 31.05 with eight hundreds. He finished as the only cricketer to pass both 400 Test wickets and 5,000 Test runs, and in 1994 he went past Richard Hadlee to hold the record for the most Test wickets.

Then there was 1983. At 24, he captained India to the World Cup. Against Zimbabwe at Tunbridge Wells, with his side in deep trouble, he made 175 not out and shared an unbroken stand of 126 for the ninth wicket with Kirmani. In the final he ran a long way back to hold the catch that removed Viv Richards, and India beat the West Indies.

What made him special

He had a smooth run-up and a side-on action that made the outswinger come naturally, and later he added an inswinger and a sharp inswinging yorker. He was tough, too: he never missed a Test or a one-day match on fitness grounds. With the bat he simply attacked. At Lord's in 1990, with India needing runs to avoid the follow-on, he hit Eddie Hemmings for four sixes in a row.

He was honest about his limits. In the mid-1980s he admitted that the leg-cutter was the one delivery he could never produce to order, which left him only every other kind to work with. He was a sporting captain as well. At the 1987 World Cup he agreed that Australia's total should go up by two after a six had been signalled as a four, and India went on to lose by a single run.

Away from the middle

He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year in 1983, received the Padma Shri and the Padma Bhushan, and in 2002 Wisden named him India's Cricketer of the Century. He joined the ICC Hall of Fame in 2010. He took up golf in 1993, was a founding member of the Laureus Foundation, and in 2019 the Sports University of Haryana chose him as its first chancellor.

He has also had a quiet film career, playing himself in Iqbal in 2005.

And finally

When the film 83 told the story of that World Cup, Ranveer Singh played Kapil Dev. Kapil himself appeared too, as a spectator, which may be the only time he has watched that final from the stands.
